title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)
content:
If you have a personal Google AI subscription, all your saved chat history in Gemini can be used for training and there is no way to opt out unless you turn off chat history or use temporary chat sessions. These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers. Although Google claims to disconnect them from your account when human-reviewed, they explicitly warn 
not to enter confidential information
.
https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16836988
“[Gemini app activity] is used to improve Google services for everyone, including by training generative AI models, if your Keep Activity setting is on.“
https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#human_review
“A subset of chats are reviewed by human reviewers”
https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_retain_data
“Chats reviewed by human reviewers [...] are not deleted when you delete your activity. Instead, they are retained for up to three years.”
https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_data_usage
“Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services, including machine-learning technologies.”
To disable their training on your chat sessions, you need to turn off “Keep Activity” in Gemini’s settings. Turning that off means you’ll lose any chat sessions after 72 hours.
I learned this too late, thinking that having a paid subscription = not being turned into the product. Apparently paying is not enough.
Thank you to this user on HN for mentioning in another thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50355424

report.summary: Google's Gemini uses subscribers' saved chat history to train its models, with no opt-out except disabling chat history, and human reviewers may read conversations.
report.background: AI subscriptions were marketed as upgrades—faster models, longer context—but Google classifies consumer Gemini tiers (Google AI Pro/Ultra) as consumer services, not enterprise products. That distinction matters: Workspace and Cloud customers get data-processing addenda that exclude their content from model training, while personal accounts fall under the general Google Privacy Policy, where 'Gemini Apps Activity' is collected to 'improve Google services,' including training. This follows Google's consolidation of Bard/Gemini activity into a single 'Keep Activity' toggle. Competitors are not dramatically different—OpenAI trains on consumer ChatGPT data unless users opt out, and offers Temporary Chats—but the recurring theme has been users assuming that paying changes the data relationship. EU and UK regulators have been scrutinizing consent and purpose limitation for AI training, though enforcement lags. The Hacker News post is a documentation-driven PSA: the terms already say this; most subscribers never read them.
key_points: Paying doesn't buy privacy. Google AI Pro/Ultra subscriptions sit under consumer terms, not the enterprise data-processing agreements used by Workspace. With 'Keep Activity' on—the default—saved Gemini chats are used to train generative models. The only way out is disabling activity keeping or using Temporary Chat, neither of which the subscription UI advertises.

The opt-out is all-or-nothing. Turning off Keep Activity stops training on your chats, but Google removes Gemini chat history after 72 hours, so you lose conversational continuity. Subscribers must choose between persistent history and exclusion from training; there is no per-conversation or per-topic exemption.

Humans may read your chats. Google's docs state a subset of chats is reviewed by human reviewers, that reviewed chats are de-identified but retained up to three years, and that deleting your activity does not remove them. Google explicitly warns not to enter confidential information 'you wouldn't want a reviewer to see.'

The asymmetry versus business tiers. Workspace, Vertex AI and enterprise customers get contractual no-training guarantees and data residency; individuals pay for the same models with weaker protections. For developers prototyping on personal accounts, client code, proprietary prompts and internal documents can end up in training corpora.

It's disclosed, not hidden—but effectively invisible. Everything is on Google's support pages; the failure is UX and expectation-setting. There is no in-product notice at signup or billing, and no per-chat indicator showing whether a session is training-eligible.
report.impact: For the industry, this reinforces a two-tier data bargain: enterprise contracts with no-training clauses, consumer tiers subsidizing model improvement with conversation data. Expect louder pressure for privacy-by-default consumer tiers, clearer labeling, and possible regulatory attention under GDPR's purpose-limitation and transparency rules. For developers, the practical lesson is to treat consumer AI accounts as untrusted channels—never paste credentials, unreleased code or customer PII, and use API or enterprise endpoints (or local models) for sensitive work. For regular users, the takeaway is procedural: know where the 'Keep Activity' toggle lives, use Temporary Chat for anything personal or work-confidential, and stop assuming a monthly fee implies confidentiality. The deeper risk is trust erosion—if paying customers learn their chats feed training and human review, adoption of AI assistants for sensitive tasks may slow.
report.tools: Audit and control: Google My Activity (myactivity.google.com) to view or delete Gemini activity, Google Takeout to export it, the 'Keep Activity' toggle in Gemini settings, and Temporary Chat for off-the-record sessions. For sensitive work, prefer endpoints with no-training guarantees (paid Gemini API, Vertex AI, OpenAI API/Enterprise, Anthropic API) or run models locally via Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp and Open WebUI. Privacy-forward hosted options include DuckDuckGo AI Chat (anonymized) and Mistral's Le Chat.
